markdownRemark.html:
Blue to yellow should be easy: two colors, a smooth blend between them. In most programs the middle is a dead, muddy gray. This is the practical part of my color series: which color space does the math of a gradient happen in, and why does it matter?

It builds on the rest of the series: the instruction an RGB number is, the map of visible color, HSL and Lab. You can read it without them, because I recap the pieces I need.

  • How does a gradient work? What is the formula?
  • Why does the same pair of colors give five different gradients?
  • What do real tools (CSS, Photoshop, Affinity) actually do?

The color series: 1. What an RGB number actually means · 2. Where the horseshoe comes from · 3. HSL and HSV: RGB with different knobs · 4. Lab: numbers that match what you see · 5. Why gradients go muddy (you are here)

Disclaimer: Same deal as in the rest of the series: I’m learning in public, guided by Claude, and I accept that I might get something wrong. I recomputed every number in the text, and I say where I tested something in a real tool and where I didn’t. If your results differ from mine, tell me in the comments. I’d rather be corrected than be confidently wrong.

Key takeaways:

  • A gradient is always the same formula, c(t) = (1 − t)·A + t·B. What changes is which three numbers A and B are written in, and that changes the middle completely.
  • Blue to yellow has five different middles: dead gray (encoded sRGB), a lighter gray (linear light), a green (HSL), a mauve (Lab) and a blue-gray (Oklab).
  • The muddy gray is a path that goes straight through the gray axis. Encoded sRGB and linear light do. Lab and Oklab walk around it.
  • If your tool lets you choose the space, choose it on purpose. If it doesn’t, find out which one it uses, or measure it.

The pieces I need from the rest of the series

A gradient between two hex colors involves four ideas I covered before. In one line each:

  • Encoded sRGB is what the hex numbers are. Stored 128 is only about 22% of the light of 255 (exposure article).
  • Linear light is the same color as amounts of light, which is what lights and lenses really add up.
  • HSL is RGB relabelled as hue, saturation and lightness (HSL and HSV).
  • Lab and Oklab are coordinates built so distances match what you see, with a real lightness L* and gray at a* = b* = 0 (Lab).

How a gradient works

When a tool draws a gradient from color A to color B, the math is always the same: a straight-line blend between two points,

c(t) = (1 − t)·A + t·B, t from 0 to 1

The formula never changes. What changes is which three numbers A and B are written in. A straight line in one space is a curve in another.

Here it is for blue to yellow, in five spaces. Each bar is computed with my own code (so it looks the same in every browser), and the position slider shows the exact color in each:

Interactive illustration (gradient-spaces). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

Look at the middles:

  • Encoded sRGB: #808080. Dead gray. This is the “muddy middle”: blue and yellow are opposite on the channels, so they cancel each other out.
  • Linear light: #BCBCBC. A lighter gray. Averaging the light itself is what overlapping lights really do, and it is the right thing for blurs and bloom, but for a gradient it looks too bright.
  • HSL: #00FF80. It walks around the hue wheel, so it never goes gray, but blue and yellow are exactly 180° apart, so the direction is a coin toss (I followed the rule CSS uses for that tie, and it goes through cyan and green).
  • Lab: #CA8AAA. The lightness changes evenly now, and the line between the two colors passes the gray point at a distance instead of through it, which leaves a mauve (L* 65, chroma 30).
  • Oklab: #6CABC7. A blue-gray with a hint of teal.

Red to green shows another side of it:

Interactive illustration (gradient-spaces). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

Encoded sRGB gives a muddy dark olive (#808000), linear light a brighter one (#BCBC00). HSL gives a bright yellow (#FFFF00) because it passes through the hue between them, but its lightness jumps around. Lab and Oklab give #C9AB00 and #D0A800. The Lab one is marked “clipped”: that midpoint is a color sRGB can’t show, so my code squeezes it into range.

And black to white, where there is no color at all:

Interactive illustration (gradient-spaces). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

All the same endpoints, and the middle gray is #808080, #BCBCBC, #777777 or #636363, depending on the space. “Middle gray” is not one color: L* 50 is #777777 and Oklab’s 0.5 is #636363.

Pro Tip: If a gradient in your editor looks muddy or too bright in the middle, it is probably doing its blend in encoded sRGB or in linear light. The fix is not a different gradient, it is a different space for the math, if your tool lets you choose.

Why the middle goes gray

A gradient is a path, and a path can be drawn. Here are the same five blends from above, drawn on the a*/b* plane of Lab (looking straight down the lightness axis, so lightness is not shown). The gray cross in the middle is where color disappears:

Interactive illustration (gradient-path). Open this article on antondanshin.com to try it.

I measured how close each path gets to the gray point, along the whole gradient (chroma is the distance from it):

  • Encoded sRGB and linear light go through it: chroma 0 at exactly 50%. That is the dead gray. They differ only in how light the gray is (L* 54 and 76).
  • HSL swings far out, never closer than a chroma of 44, because it walks around the hue wheel. That is why it stays vivid, and why it shoots through green.
  • Lab and Oklab pass it at a distance, never closer than a chroma of 23 and 19 (both at about 58%). That is what keeps the hint of color in their middles.

So “muddy” has a precise meaning here: a path that crosses the gray axis. Blue and yellow sit on opposite sides of it, so the straight line between them in encoded sRGB or linear light runs straight through.

What real tools do

I wanted to know what actual tools do, and this is as far as I got.

  • CSS in a browser. In the browser I tested (Chrome 152, November 2026), a gradient between two plain hex colors blended in encoded sRGB, so blue to yellow went through gray. Modern color syntaxes such as oklab() default to Oklab, and linear-gradient(in oklab, …) asks for it on any colors. The standard has changed its mind on this more than once, so check your own browser; MDN documents the in keyword. As a check on my code: the browser’s own color-mix(in oklab, #0000ff, #ffff00) gives oklab(0.710, −0.0519, −0.0565), the same color as my Oklab middle. The same check agrees with my encoded sRGB, linear light and HSL middles too. The exception is Lab: CSS’s lab() is defined with a D50 white point (the print industry’s), while mine is the textbook D65 Lab that matches sRGB’s white, so in lab in a browser gives a slightly different mauve for blue to yellow (#C289AC instead of my #CA8AAA). Same idea, a slightly different white.
  • Photoshop. I don’t use it, so this is from Adobe’s own announcement: the gradient tool has a Method option with Classic (the document’s working space), Linear (linear light) and Perceptual (which Adobe says uses Oklab, and which is the default in newer versions).
  • Affinity Photo. I haven’t measured it, so I can’t tell you. If you’d like to find out: draw a black-to-white gradient, sample the center, and see if it reads 128 (encoded sRGB), 188 (linear light) or 119 (Lab).

Gradient maps are two calculations

One more thing I want to keep in mind. A gradient map (the adjustment that recolors a photo by brightness) does two things: it reduces every pixel to one gray value, which is where it looks up the gradient, and then it blends between the stops at that position. Both steps depend on a choice of space. This is my reasoning, not something I measured: if you put a stop “near the middle gray”, it only lands where you expect if the tool measures that middle gray the same way you do.

If you want to try this on your own colors, there is a small tool page with a gradient comparison where you can pick any two colors. It also prints the CSS line that asks a browser for each of the five blends, ready to copy.

What I took away

A gradient is one formula, and the only decision is which numbers it runs on. Blue to yellow has five different middles because a straight line in one space is a curve in another, and the muddy gray is simply the path that crosses the gray axis. If you remember one thing: before you trust a gradient tool, find out which space it does its math in, or measure it.

What I’d keep from the whole series:

  1. A color number means nothing until you know its space.
  2. Bits give resolution; primaries give range.
  3. HSL and HSV are for picking colors, not for judging lightness.
  4. Perceptual spaces (Lab, Oklab) are for comparing, masking and making smooth ramps.
  5. Linear light is for physics: mixing light, blur, bloom.
  6. Before you trust a tool, find out which space it does its math in, or measure it.

The series, in order: What an RGB number actually means, Where the horseshoe comes from, HSL and HSV, Lab, and this one. It all started in Exposure vs Brightness.

Next I want to look at contrast. It has the same “no standard” problem as brightness, plus a new question: which tone does it pivot around?

Did I get something wrong, or do you use color differently? The comments are open.
